cards.front: Worked example (§4): \(P_1=8.0\%\), \(P_2\text{R}=2.0\%\) of TREA, CBR \(=3.5\%\), SRB-default MCC \(=\) CBR \(-125\,\text{bps}\). Compute the risk-weighted MREL ratio \(\text{MREL}_{\text{RWA}}=2(P_1+P_2\text{R})+\text{MCC}\) (as a fraction of TREA).
SRB-default market confidence charge (Marktvertrauenspuffer) with CBR \(=3.5\%\): \(\text{MCC}=\text{CBR}-125\,\text{bps}\), floored at zero. Give the MCC as a fraction of TREA.

Resolution entity: binding MREL \(=\)EUR 940m, holds EUR 700m CET1 + EUR 300m non-CET1 subordinated eligible debt, CBR \(=\)EUR 140m. Using the CET1-specific test (apply non-CET1 to MREL first), compute the M-MDA shortfall in euros.
Same scenario (MREL EUR 940m, CET1 held EUR 700m, non-CET1 eligible debt EUR 300m). After applying non-CET1 debt to MREL first, compute the residual CET1 available to cover the CBR, in euros.
Sector covered deposits \(=\)EUR 50,000m. DGSD/ESAEG target level is 0.8% of covered deposits. Compute the target available financial means, in euros.

A primary bank with EUR 500m covered deposits, sector-average annual levy 0.05% of covered deposits, aggregate risk weight ARW \(=0.75\). Compute its illustrative annual risk-based DGS contribution: \(0.05\%\times 500\text{m}\times 0.75\), in euros.
MREL has two legs: MREL = {{c1}} + {{c2}}. The {{c1}} answers 'how much loss must be absorbed to reach failure' (= P1+P2R); the {{c2}} answers 'how much capital rebuilds viability' (= P1+P2R+MCC).

DGSD/ESAEG cold figures: coverage level {{c1}} EUR per depositor per institution; fund target {{c2}} of covered deposits; payout deadline {{c3}} working days; and under BRRD Art. 109 a capped DGS contribution in resolution of at most {{c4}} of the target level.
Walk the CET1-specific M-MDA check. Inputs: binding MREL EUR 940m, CET1 held EUR 700m, non-CET1 subordinated eligible debt EUR 300m, CBR EUR 140m.

steps.prompt: How much MREL must be met with CET1, after applying non-CET1 eligible debt first?
steps.expected: 940 - 300 = EUR 640m of CET1 consumed by MREL
steps.explain: Non-CET1 subordinated eligible debt is applied to MREL first; the remainder of MREL must be filled with CET1.

steps.prompt: What is the residual CET1 left to cover the CBR?
steps.explain: Only CET1 not already spent on MREL is available for the CBR — the same euro cannot be spent twice.

steps.prompt: What is the M-MDA shortfall against the CBR?
steps.explain: The CBR (EUR 140m) must be met with CET1 on top of MREL; residual CET1 is only EUR 60m, so distributions/AT1 coupons/variable remuneration can be capped.

cards.front: Classify the spine: 'A Niederösterreich primary bank carries a liquidation strategy (negative PIA) and the sector backs that outcome with R-IPS/DGS mutual support.' Is the driver reg, ÖRS, or mixed — and produce the tradeoff that decision creates?
rubric: the produced tradeoff point: the PIA outcome itself is REG (BRRD Art. 32(5)/SRMR Art. 18(5) force liquidation when ordinary insolvency meets the resolution objectives to the same extent — functions substitutable, deposits DGS-protected), but how the sector organises mutual support around that outcome is an ÖRS modelling decision
names the cost saved: liquidation strategy ⇒ no external MREL beyond own funds ⇒ no costly subordinated-debt programme at the primary level (post Directive 2024/1174)
names the cost incurred: the burden of preventing failure shifts onto the R-IPS and DGS — cheaper in capital, heavier in mutual solidarity
notes the PIA is decided by substitutability, NOT balance-sheet size: a large bank can fail it, a small one can pass it

cards.front: Two routes to the M-MDA shortfall both yield EUR 80m: (A) compare total eligible instruments EUR 1,000m against a stacked MREL+CBR of EUR 1,080m; (B) apply non-CET1 debt to MREL first, then test residual CET1 (EUR 60m) against the CBR (EUR 140m). Which is methodologically correct, and produce the tradeoff/error?
rubric: the produced tradeoff point: route B is the only correct route — the M-MDA test (BRRD2 Art. 16a) is CET1-specific; the CBR can ONLY be met with CET1 not already spent on MREL

identifies route A's silent error: comparing total instruments against a stacked MREL+CBR figure lets the EUR 300m non-CET1 subordinated debt implicitly count toward the CBR — the double-counting M-MDA exists to forbid
notes the two give the same number here only by coincidence; under other input mixes route A misstates the shortfall
consequence: model CET1 as a scarce resource (non-CET1 to MREL first, CET1 fills the rest, residual CET1 vs CBR) — never two independent ratios checked in parallel

cards.front: Distinguish recovery (Sanierung), early intervention (frühzeitiges Eingreifen), and resolution (Abwicklung) — who acts, on what trigger, and what sits between an indicator breach and a FOLTF determination?

rubric.text: Recovery/Sanierungsplan: written by the BANK, assumes survival (going concern), approved by the supervisor; a recovery-indicator breach triggers MANAGEMENT escalation, not resolution

Early intervention (BRRD Art. 27–29, transposed in BaSAG): a SUPERVISORY going-concern power filling the gap before FOLTF — force execution of the recovery plan (Art. 27), remove/replace management (Art. 28), appoint a temporary administrator / vorläufiger Verwalter (Art. 29)
Resolution/Abwicklungsplan: written by the RESOLUTION AUTHORITY (SRB/FMA), assumes failure; opened only on FOLTF (Art. 32) PLUS a positive public-interest assessment
States the full ladder: indicator breach → management escalation → supervisory early intervention → FOLTF → resolution or liquidation

antiPoints: Claiming a recovery-indicator breach itself triggers resolution (skips the middle rungs and makes failure look like a cliff)
Saying the bank writes the resolution plan, or the authority writes the recovery plan (authors are reversed)
Treating early intervention as a gone-concern/resolution tool rather than a going-concern supervisory power
cards.modelAnswer: Recovery is what the bank does to save itself: it authors a living Sanierungsplan (BRRD Art. 5, BaSAG) assuming survival, with calibrated indicators whose breach triggers management escalation, not resolution. Between an indicator breach and a 'failing or likely to fail' determination sits supervisory early intervention (BRRD Art. 27–29): the FMA/SSM can force execution of the recovery plan, replace the management body (Art. 28), or install a vorläufiger Verwalter (Art. 29) while the bank is still a going concern. Resolution is different in kind — the resolution authority authors the Abwicklungsplan assuming failure, and it opens only on FOLTF (Art. 32) plus a positive public-interest assessment; the bank merely supplies data. Different documents, different authors, different worlds.

cards.front: Defend to the Aufsichtsrat the sector's three-way safety net — R-IPS vs DGS vs resolution. Which bites first, who pays at each layer, and what is the proportionality bargain?

rubric.text: R-IPS bites FIRST and hardest: a going-concern PREVENTION tool that can inject capital/liquidity into a wobbling member before FOLTF — upstream even of supervisory early intervention; paid by the sector members mutually
DGS (ESAEG) acts AFTER failure: payout of covered deposits (≤ 7 working days, EUR 100,000) OR a capped contribution in resolution (BRRD Art. 109); paid from the ex-ante levied fund
Resolution (SRB/FMA) is last and essentially never used for primary banks: requires FOLTF + positive PIA; loss borne by shareholders & creditors (bail-in), then the SRF

Names the proportionality bargain/tradeoff: a healthy IPS means members rarely reach FOLTF, so MREL is near-absent at the primary level — capital-cheap, but paid for by pre-funded mutual solidarity rather than market-funded bail-in

antiPoints: Putting resolution or DGS payout first in the sequence (the IPS acts upstream of both)
Claiming the State's resolution tools are the sector's primary backstop
Saying the DGS is only a payout vehicle and never contributes in resolution (ignores BRRD Art. 109)
cards.modelAnswer: The sector runs three overlapping mechanisms in a deliberate order. The R-IPS bites first: as a going-concern prevention tool it can recapitalise or fund a wobbling member before it ever reaches FOLTF — upstream even of supervisory early intervention — and it is paid for mutually by the members. The DGS (ESAEG) is the next layer, acting after failure: it pays covered deposits up to EUR 100,000 within seven working days, and under BRRD Art. 109 it can also be required to contribute in a resolution, capped by the NCWO counterfactual and 50% of its target level. Resolution by the SRB/FMA is the last layer and essentially never reached for a primary bank, since it needs FOLTF plus a positive PIA; there shareholders and creditors bear losses via bail-in before the SRF. The defensible board narrative: we do not rely on the State's resolution tools because we have priced and pre-funded mutual support that stops failures upstream — that is the proportionality bargain, and it is exactly why MREL is near-absent at the primary level.
